judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in the Listening and Speaking (Oral) Skill Area and both use pictorial cues as a basis for oral expression. The second SFI (Grade R, rank 0, Term 2, sub-strand 'Uses visual and pictorial cues to make meaning') is 'Looks carefully at pictures and talks about common experiences', with LCs 'Looks carefully at pictures' and 'Talks about common experiences'. judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade 3, Term 4, Skill Area 'READING AND PHONICS' (same rank 3, same term), but under different printed sub-strands: the first under 'Group Guided Reading:' ('Reads both silently and out loud from own book in a guided reading group with the teacher; whole group reads the same story at the instructional level of the group') and the second under 'Paired/Independent Reading' ('Reads independently at a more complex level for enjoyment or information from a variety of available texts...'). This is not generic repetition: the pair differs in support and text demand. Teacher-scaffolded reading of a common story pitched at the group's instructional level develops the decoding fluency and silent/oral reading stamina that make success at unsupported, self-selected reading of more complex and more varied texts (magazines, comics, fiction/non-fiction, Shared Reading books) more likely, so proficiency in the guided-reading skill supports the independent-reading skill. Same-grade, same-term direction is permitted and is justified by the scaffolded-to-independent and instructional-to-more-complex shift rather than by shared ancestry, page proximity, or the shared 'reading' token alone. Endpoint source evidence and the first SFI's LC evidence are truncated, limiting the excerpt but not the printed statement text relied on here.

judgment.rationale: First is Grade R, Term 2, Emergent Reading / 'Emergent reading skills': 'Develops correct eye movement such as following a ball moved from left to right' (LC tags: eye movement, left to right, tracking). Second is Grade R, Term 3, Emergent Writing / Handwriting: 'Begins to form letters: uses finger painting, paint brushes, wax crayons, pegboards or elastic boards' (LC tags: fine motor, handwriting, letter formation). Both are Grade R (rank 0) emergent-literacy perceptual-motor foundations and the term order (Term 2 before Term 3) would permit a forward direction, but the evidence shows two different capabilities in different skill areas: ocular tracking/directionality for reading versus fine-motor mark-making for letter formation. Nothing in the supplied statements or LCs asserts that visual tracking proficiency supports success in forming letters with painting/crayon/pegboard tools, and the nomination signals are weak (shared Grade ancestor, rank gap 0, LC tag overlap only on the generic token 'emergent', text Jaccard ~0.04). This is substantive complementary coherence within Grade R emergent literacy rather than a justified developmental dependency, so relatesTo is the supported judgment. judgment.rationale: Both are distinct printed bullets under the same Grade 3, Term 1, WRITING / Handwriting sub-strand (page 113), so there is no cross-term or cross-grade ordering; direction rests on the substantive content difference. The first SFI covers forming all lower- and upper-case letters in joined/cursive script and only 'begins' to join letters and form words (LCs: forms all letters; begins to join various letters; begins to form words). Same-rank direction is justified by this capability expansion (letters/emergent joins -> complete short words), not by shared wording, shared parent, or page proximity. judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are Grade R (rank 0), Term 4, Skill Area EMERGENT READING bullets printed in the same table cell, but under different sub-strands: "'Reads' picture books of increasing complexity" (Emergent reading skills) and "Answers a range of questions based on the story read" (Shared Reading). They are substantively coherent emergent meaning-making-from-text skills: independently 'reading'/interpreting picture books and orally responding to comprehension questions about a shared story reinforce the same emergent-literacy construct of deriving meaning from texts. However, the evidence shows them as parallel same-grade, same-term expectations in different sub-strands, with no indication that proficiency in one is developmentally required for or expands into the other (token/trigram overlap is trivial — only 'of' and 'rea'/'ead'), so no substantive same-rank developmental direction is supported. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each) and both carry upstream audit/merge context, which limits but does not contradict this reading; the symmetric relatesTo judgment is the safest supported outcome.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade 1 Listening and Speaking (Oral) Skills: the first (Term 1, 'Daily / Weekly activities' sub-strand) is 'Talks about personal experiences: tells news, describes weather news, other topical events etc.', the second (Term 2, 'Twice weekly focussed listening and speaking activities' sub-strand) is 'Describes objects in terms of age, direction, sequence using correct vocabulary'. They cohere substantively as complementary oral expression/description skills (LC tags 'oral', 'speaking' vs 'oral', 'describing', 'vocabulary'), and the Term 1 to Term 2 order would permit a forward buildsTowards. However, the two target different objects of description: free personal/topical news-telling versus focussed, precise descriptive vocabulary for attributes of objects. The evidence shows only weak lexical overlap (single shared token 'describes', jaccard 0.05) and no indication that competence in telling news is needed for, or specifically enables, accurate attribute vocabulary; they sit in different sub-strands of the same skill area. Meaningful reinforcement within oral language supports relatesTo rather than a developmental dependency. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each) and all endpoints and ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, so the judgment rests on the bounded excerpts supplied.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs sit in the WRITING skill area. The second SFI is Grade 1, Term 3 (Handwriting sub-strand): 'Copies and writes short sentences correctly', with LCs 'Copies short sentences correctly' and 'Writes short sentences correctly'. The first SFI is Grade 3, Term 4 (Shared, Group and Independent Writing): 'Uses conjunctions to form compound sentences'. Coordinates are resolved (rank 1 to rank 3), so the only permitted developmental direction is lower-to-higher, i.e. second_to_first. This is substantive extension rather than generic repetition: accurately producing single short sentences is the enabling capability for joining clauses with conjunctions into longer compound sentences, moving from copying/correct sentence production to independent grammatical combination. Note the Grade 1 statement's sub-strand is Handwriting (mechanical accuracy focus), so the support is partial rather than a strict prerequisite, which is consistent with buildsTowards semantics. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated and both carry upstream audit/merge context; the retained statement text and identity scopes were sufficient and unambiguous for this judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade R (rank 0) Emergent Reading Skills, but they address different emergent-literacy constructs: the first (Term 4, Shared Reading sub-strand) is a concepts-of-print behaviour — 'Points at words rather than pictures when "reading"' (LC tags: print awareness, pointing, words); the second (Term 3, Phonological/Phonemic Awareness sub-strand) is oral segmentation — dividing multisyllabic words into syllables with claps/drumbeats and counting them (LC tags: phonological awareness, syllables, counting). They are nonetheless coherent, complementary emergent-reading strands both concerned with treating the word as a unit (orally and in print), supporting relatesTo. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each) and both carry upstream audit/merge context, so a stronger developmental claim is not supportable from this bounded evidence.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade 3 (rank 3), Term 1, Skill Area WRITING, but under different sub-strands: Handwriting ('Forms all lower and upper-case letters in joined script or cursive writing and begins to join various letters and to form words') versus Shared, Group and Independent Writing ('Draws pictures and writes sentences to show understanding of a story'). They are coherent complementary strands of written production - transcription/letter formation alongside composing sentences and drawing in response to a story - so there is genuine instructional coherence. However, the evidence does not support a developmental dependency in either direction at the same grade and same term: the cursive/joining skill is an emerging ('begins to') new script skill whose mastery is not required to write sentences about a story (the Grade 3 Term 1 table context even notes children may still be using print script in written recording until the end of the second term), and composing sentences about a story does not develop joined-script letter formation. Same-rank, same-term direction would need substantive evidence that is absent here, and the nomination signals (shared ancestors, same page, token overlap limited to 'and'/'to' and generic 'writ-' trigrams) are not semantic evidence. Endpoint source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade 3 WRITING > Handwriting skills about joined/cursive script for all written recording, but the source identity scopes differ by term: the second SFI is Grade 3 Term 2 ('Makes transition to the joined script or cursive writing in all written recording, that is, the date, own name, and own written texts'), while the first SFI is Grade 3 Term 4 ('Uses the joined script or cursive writing for all written recording'). This is substantive progression, not mere repeated wording: Term 2 frames the move from print script to joined script with scaffolded exemplars (date, own name, own texts), whereas Term 4 expects consolidated, unqualified use of joined script across all written recording (Term 4 row context emphasises increasing writing speed while maintaining neatness and legibility). Proficiency in making the transition supports success in habitual, fluent use, so buildsTowards runs from the earlier Term 2 node (second) to the later Term 4 node (first), consistent with the within-grade earlier-to-later term constraint. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated and both carry upstream audit/merge context, but the retained statement text, term scopes and Handwriting sub-strand placement are sufficient and non-conflicting.

judgment.rationale: First SFI is a Grade 3 Term 3 Listening and Speaking (Oral) bullet, 'Interviews people for a particular purpose such as to find out about a person's work' (sub-strand: Twice weekly focussed listening and speaking activities); second is a Grade 3 Term 4 Writing bullet, 'Writes a selection of short texts for different purposes such as recounts, dialogues' (sub-strand: Shared, Group and Independent Writing). They cohere substantively around purpose-driven language use — gathering information orally through questioning and producing short written texts (including recounts and dialogues) matched to a purpose — so they reinforce each other across the oral and written modes. However, the evidence shows no dependency: interviewing skill is not presented as supporting written text production, and the nomination signals are largely shared-grade hierarchy, the single shared LC tag 'purpose', and generic token/trigram overlap ('a', 'as', 'for', 'such'), which alone cannot establish developmental direction. Term 3 to Term 4 ordering within Grade 3 would permit a forward buildsTowards, but the cross-skill-area evidence is too thin to assert that proficiency in interviewing supports success in writing varied short texts, so the symmetric relation is the better-supported judgment. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), limiting the view of the full bullet context.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs sit under Grade 1 (rank 1) Reading and Phonics. The second SFI is Grade 1 Term 1, Sub-strand Phonics: 'Recognises and names some letters of the alphabet: 2 vowels and at least 6 consonants' (LCs: recognises letters; names letters). The first SFI is Grade 1 Term 2, Sub-strand Group Guided Reading: 'Reads aloud from own book in a guided reading group with teacher, that is, the whole group reads the same story'. Initial letter-sound recognition and naming is the decoding foundation that supports successfully reading aloud connected text from one's own book in a guided group, so the earlier-Term 1 phonics skill builds towards the later-Term 2 oral reading skill (second_to_first, a permitted earlier-to-later direction within Grade 1). This is substantive complementary progression within the same Skill Area, not mere wording overlap (shared tokens are only 'the'/'ame'/'s a', which carry no semantic weight). Source evidence excerpts for both endpoints are truncated and both endpoints and their ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, so the judgment rests on the full statement texts, identity scopes (Term 1 vs Term 2) and LC evidence supplied.

This is substantive conceptual coherence around story sense in Grade R, complementary rather than dependent; the Term 2→Term 3 ordering alone does not evidence that picture-'reading' supports success in listening comprehension of longer stories, so relatesTo is the supported judgment. The second SFI states foundational print-concept knowledge ('Understands that print communicates meaning. Knows words can represent own name, names of people, places and things'; LCs tagged print awareness, meaning, names/words). The first SFI applies that insight to actual recognition of specific written word forms ('‘Reads’ high frequency words: peer names, calendar and weather words'; LC tagged high frequency words, sight words). Knowing that printed words carry meaning and can stand for people's names plausibly supports success in sight-reading peer names and calendar/weather words, so proficiency in the second supports the first; this is a within-term developmental link, not mere wording overlap ('names', 'words') or shared-parent proximity. Evidence limits: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all nodes carry upstream audit/merge context, so judgment rests on the bounded statement text and LCs.
